title: Growing rocket microgreens
subtitle: Peppery salad-leaf cotyledons ready in 7 to 10 days
excerpt: Rocket microgreens produce the same peppery, slightly nutty flavour as mature rocket leaves but at the cotyledon stage, without the toughening or bitterness that develops in summer outdoor rocket. Sow on a 25 cm tray and cut in 7 to 10 days.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides. Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: Watering by setting the growing tray inside a second tray filled with water, allowing the growing medium to draw moisture up from below. Keeps the seedling surface dry and reduces mould and damping-off risk in microgreen trays.

A fungal condition where seedling stems collapse and rot at the soil surface. Caused by Pythium, Fusarium, and Rhizoctonia species in warm, wet, poorly-ventilated conditions. Common in overcrowded or overwatered microgreen trays.

content.text: Rocket microgreens are a year-round indoor tray crop that reaches the cutting stage in 7 to 10 days. Sow densely on a 25 cm tray, blackout for two to three days to push straight stems, then bring to light and cut with scissors when the cotyledons are fully open. The flavour is peppery and mild, without the bitterness that outdoor rocket picks up in hot weather.

Light: a bright windowsill in spring and summer. In winter, a supplementary LED grow light 15 to 20 cm above the tray, running 14 hours a day, produces a more upright, uniformly green tray. Rocket microgreens in low winter light stay pale longer after the blackout phase but green up acceptably given a few extra days.
Temperature: 16 to 22°C. Rocket grows well at slightly lower temperatures than basil or coriander; it can tolerate a cool kitchen corner in spring without slowing significantly.

Day 0: sow. Pre-dampen seed compost or coir and fill the tray to within 1 cm of the rim. Scatter rocket seed at 15 to 20 g per 25 cm tray; the seed is small and light, so sow with a shaker motion from 20 to 30 cm above the surface for even distribution. Press gently into contact with the medium.
Days 1 to 3: blackout. Cover with a weighted second tray. Remove when shoots are 2 to 3 cm tall. Rocket typically reaches this in two to three days.
Day 4 onward: light. The cotyledons green up within 24 hours of their first light exposure.
only from this point: set the growing tray inside a second tray with 1 to 2 cm of water and let the medium draw it up. Allow the water to be absorbed before adding more.
Days 7 to 10: cut. When cotyledons are fully open, green, and 5 to 8 cm tall, cut 1 cm above the medium surface with sharp scissors. Rinse, spin, use fresh or refrigerate for up to two days.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common problems with rocket microgreen trays.

items.symptom: Stems wet and limp, base collapses
items.cause: Damping off from top-watering or stagnant moisture.
items.fix: Bottom-water only. Discard the affected tray; damping off spreads through a dense tray quickly. Restart.

items.symptom: Slow germination, sparse coverage after day 4
items.cause: Old seed stock or medium too dry during the germination window.
items.fix: Check seed viability. Ensure the medium is uniformly damp (not wet) before sowing. The germination medium should feel like a well-wrung sponge.

items.symptom: Pale, thin stems that fall over after the blackout phase
items.cause: Blackout left on too long, or insufficient light after moving out.
items.fix: Remove the cover as soon as shoots are 2 to 3 cm tall. Move to a brighter position or add a grow light.

content.text: Use untreated rocket seed. Standard vegetable rocket seed is usually fungicide-free (it is sold for home salad growing), but check with the supplier when buying in bulk for microgreen trays. Microgreen suppliers sell rocket seed in larger packs suited to tray growing.
is the main risk on rocket trays, as on all microgreen trays. The preventive measures are the same: bottom-water only, good airflow, seed compost rather than potting compost.
